name: The Microphones
label: K
lede: Phil Elverum recorded his first Microphones tapes in the back room of an Anacortes record store, then took them to Olympia and K Records. He ran a guitar through a thrift-store cassette deck, made The Glow Pt. 2, and dropped the name in 2003. In 2020 he picked it back up for one 44-minute song.

eras.title: A back room at The Business
eras.text: Elverum is a teenager clerking at an Anacortes record store and recording in its back room. By 1998 he has moved to Olympia, and the man who runs the town's label has noticed.

years.src: Wikipedia: The Microphones · Wikipedia: Phil Elverum · Wikipedia: Tests (album)
years.h: The back room at The Business becomes a studio
years.p: Phil Elverum works at The Business, an Anacortes record store, and records in its back room. Owner Bret Lunsford puts out two Microphones cassettes on his Knw-Yr-Own label: Microphone and Wires and Cords.
years.xp:
Elverum was also drumming for Lunsford's band D+ around then. By his own account, the record store was how he got into alternative music.

Wikipedia says the Tests tapes were recorded at The Business while he worked there, and that the 1998 CD later folded that material in with newer recordings. The same store is where his high-school recording experiments happened, per Wikipedia's Don't Wake Me Up article.

years.src: Wikipedia: The Microphones · Wikipedia: Phil Elverum
years.h: Olympia pulls Elverum away from Evergreen State
years.p: He enrolls at Evergreen State College, then puts the music scene ahead of class. [[Calvin Johnson|cac7a688-14a8-46c3-8fc8-11cca866677c]], who runs K Records, starts recording him at his Dub Narcotic studio.

years.h: Tests turns the Anacortes cassettes into a CD
years.p: The Elsinor CD pairs the cassette material with new recordings made in Olympia, and it's the Microphones' first full-length. The 7-inch "Bass Drum Dream" comes out on Up Records the same year.
years.xp: Per Wikipedia, Tests began as a Knw-Yr-Own cassette and took its CD form on Elsinor Records. The same page says P.W. Elverum & Sun reissued the cassette in an edition of 20 for Record Store Day 2011, sold at The Business.

eras.title: K Records signs the kid
eras.text: Three records in two years on K, cut at Calvin Johnson's studio with a rotating cast of friends. It's all 16-track tape, so a bad take means playing it again.

years.src: Wikipedia: Don't Wake Me Up (album) · Wikipedia: The Microphones
years.h: Don't Wake Me Up turns fifteen tracks into one wall of mud
years.p: Elverum was 20 when he finished recording it, in a warehouse-sized Olympia room. Mirah, Khaela Maricich, Bronwyn Holm and Johnson sing on it.
years.xp:
Recording ran from April 1998 to March 1999, at Dub Narcotic in Olympia and at The Business in Anacortes. Pitchfork's Ryan Schreiber praised the muddy production and the way the 15 tracks blend into a single piece.

Wikipedia says the record gave K Records a new idea of what a K release could sound like, and gave Elverum his first real audience.

years.h: Mirah tours the US and Canada with the Microphones
years.p: Elverum had asked her to add guitar and vocals, and she played on Don't Wake Me Up and Window. He co-produced her 2000 debut, You Think It's Like This but Really It's Like This.

yt: The Glow Pt. 2, live in Lexington, KY, Nov. 4, 2000
years.h: A guitar through a thrift-store cassette deck starts The Glow Pt. 2
years.p: Sessions at Dub Narcotic begin May 23 and run to March 23, 2001, mostly early mornings on 16-track tape. The distortion comes from sending the guitar into the mic input of a cassette deck, out the headphone jack and into an amp.
years.xp:
Wikipedia credits [[Karl Blau|688d2d9d-8f49-4187-b558-2c961c699ab1]] as engineer and drum machine operator (the machine was a Chamberlin Rhythmate 40) and [[Khaela Maricich|07d0cdc9-6e87-4645-ba65-a042961c6e7c]] as engineer and vocalist on tracks 12 and 16. It says the end of her relationship with Elverum shaped the album's themes, and that Mirah told him in the studio it was going to be something special.

Months into the sessions, on November 4, 2000, the band played the title song live in Lexington, Kentucky (video above).

The cover art comes from a 1933-34 Dutch cookbook, Calvé-Delft's Winterboekje. Elverum has named extreme metal, ambient music and Twin Peaks among the influences, per Wikipedia.

years.src: Wikipedia: It Was Hot, We Stayed in the Water · Wikipedia: Karl Blau
years.h: It Was Hot, We Stayed in the Water lands seventh on Pitchfork's 2000 list
years.p: Recorded at Dub Narcotic between September 1999 and March 2000, it came out on K on September 26. Pitchfork gave it 9.2 and put it seventh on its Top 20 Albums of 2000.
years.xp:
Khaela Maricich wrote the song "(Something)", and Mirah sings guest vocals on "Ice". Karl Blau, an Anacortes musician on the Knw-Yr-Own side of K, also worked on the record and has a song titled after him.

Elverum said analog tape gave him a technical reason for charismatic sloppiness: re-recording a take wasn't practical.

eras.title: The Glow, then a mountain
eras.text: The record people name first, then a five-track climb up a mountain, a winter in Norway and a new name.

years.h: The Glow Pt. 2 comes out at 66 minutes, sloppy on purpose
years.p: Pitchfork gave it 9.2 on release and 9.3 for the 2008 reissue. Say Microphones to most people and this is the record they mean.
years.xp:
The album is stereo throughout, and its sprawl and noise took it from a K release to a reference point. Wikipedia lists Lil Peep, who sampled three tracks, plus Sylvan Esso, Kevin Morby and Wild Nothing's Jack Tatum among artists it influenced. The Guardian called it "a millennial Daydream Nation" in 2013.

Elverum has pushed back on the canon talk. Wikipedia quotes him saying that whether albums are good or bad or essential is "a total myth that can usually be purchased by getting a more expensive publicist." It also notes K Records kept poor records, so sales were never counted.

K put out a deluxe double CD in 2007 with 20 bonus tracks, Other Songs & Destroyed Versions, and reissued the album again on April 4, 2008, after it had gone out of print on CD and vinyl.

years.h: Song Islands sweeps up the singles and strays
years.p: Twenty-one tracks from 1998 to 2002, including "Bass Drum Dream" and "The Glow, Pt. 4". Pitchfork gave it 7.2.
years.xp: It carries both the K Records and P.W. Elverum & Sun credits (ELV 030), one of the first releases with Elverum's own imprint name on it.

years.src: Wikipedia: The Microphones · Wikipedia: Mount Eerie (album)
years.h: A long tour, then a winter in a Norwegian log cabin
years.p: After the Paper Opera Tour of Europe and North America, Elverum toured solo as "I Will Move Away Forever and Never Come Back Ever". He then spent the winter of 2002-03 in a cabin in Kjærringøy, Norway.
years.xp:
Wikipedia says he moved out of his Olympia house after recording finished, and wrote the songs that became Dawn (2008) in Norway.

He was back on the road by spring: the photo is from London in April 2003. A fan upload of a full 2002 set at Maxwell's, in Hoboken, is above.

years.h: Mount Eerie takes five tracks to climb a mountain
years.p: The album follows a climb up Mount Erie on Fidalgo Island, from womb to death, with different vocal characters. Pitchfork rated it 8.9 and Best New Music.
years.xp:
It opens with a 17-minute track, "I. The Sun". Recording ran from November 2001 to June 2002 at Dub Narcotic, with two sections done elsewhere: Kyle Field's "Big Black Death" and Karl Blau's "Wind / Vultures" at Quatro-Syncho in Trafton Lake, Washington. It came out in Japan on 7.e.p. on December 12, 2002, before the US release on K.

Elverum has said he liked the album not being the voice of one writer or a band, and that he "wanted it to be ambiguous what's going on here."

years.h: Elverum tours Japan with Johnson, Kyle Field and Moools
years.p: The tour produced Live in Japan, which K released in early 2004.

years.big: "I did it because I am ready for new things."
q: Mount Eerie is a new project.
years.src: Wikipedia: Mount Eerie · Wikipedia: Phil Elverum
years.h: Elverum retires the Microphones and starts Mount Eerie
years.p: Elverum told CITR-FM's Discorder in September 2003 that Mount Eerie, named for the hill he grew up under, was a new project. He treated it as that, not a rename.
years.xp:
The full line from the Discorder interview, as Wikipedia prints it: "Mount Eerie is a new project. The Microphones was completed, or at least at a good stopping point. I did it because I am ready for new things. I am new."

He later described both names as one progression. Wikipedia counts the Microphones years as 1996-2003.

eras.title: The back catalog goes on his own label
eras.text: Elverum records as Mount Eerie and presses the old Microphones records himself. Then his wife dies, and what he records changes.

years.h: The Glow Pt. 2 goes back to press on his own label
years.p: On July 9, the four Microphones studio albums and the singles compilation Song Islands are remastered and reissued on P.W. Elverum & Sun, the label he founded in 2004 to press, package and ship his own records.

years.src: Wikipedia: A Crow Looked at Me · Wikipedia: Geneviève Castrée
years.h: Elverum records A Crow Looked at Me in the room where his wife died
years.p: Geneviève Castrée died of pancreatic cancer on July 9, 2016. Elverum recorded the album at their Anacortes house between August and December.
years.xp:
Per Wikipedia he used one microphone, an acoustic guitar, some of her instruments and a laptop, and chose the room so it wouldn't be defined only by her last days. Recording ran from August 31 to December 6, 2016, and it came out March 24, 2017, on P.W. Elverum & Sun.

The New York Times' Jon Caramanica wrote that "the line is blurred between singing, speaking and raw emotional data dump." Elverum said he was trying "to distil all the mass of words in my head into something a little more poetic and musical."

Elverum and Castrée had married in 2004 and had one child, born in 2015.

eras.title: The name comes out of the drawer
eras.text: Elverum plays one hometown show as the Microphones, then makes a single record about the name.

years.p: Elverum plays the hometown show in June 2019, with D+, Black Belt Eagle Scout and Little Wings on the bill.

years.h: Microphones in 2020 is one 44:44 song about being Phil Elverum
years.p: He announced it June 16 and recorded it between May 2019 and May 2020. Pitchfork gave it 8.5 and Best New Music.
years.xp:
It opens with about seven minutes of instrumental, two double-tracked chords, before speak-singing, drums, bass, organ, electric guitar and piano arrive. Wikipedia says it looks back over his career and includes a nod to The Glow Pt. 2.

Elverum on the concept: "Here I am right now in 2020. I am currently all of those things." He also said he thinks of it "more as an audiobook or something."

He left it off Spotify as a protest against the streaming business model, per Wikipedia. Metacritic lists 87 from seven reviews. He played it live on limited dates in 2021 and 2022.

yt: Full set, Lodge Room, Los Angeles, 2022
years.h: A box set, and the last Microphones release
years.p: On January 13, Elverum announces Completely Everything, 1996–2021, a box set gathering the whole run, and says it will be the final Microphones release.
years.xp: Wikipedia says he played the new album live on limited dates in 2021 and 2022 before putting the name away again. The video above is a full set from the Lodge Room in Los Angeles in 2022.
